questions.prompt: Why can't two agents safely work on different features in the SAME checkout at the same time?

options.text: Git forbids two processes in one directory
They share the same working files — edits collide, and one agent's half-done changes contaminate the other's builds and tests
Two agents would double the API cost
They can — files are locked automatically

questions.explanation: A working directory is shared mutable state. Agent A's in-progress edits sit in Agent B's view of the world; tests, builds, and edits interleave chaotically.

questions.prompt: What does `git worktree add` give you?

options.text: A full second copy of the repository history on another disk
An additional working directory with its own checked-out branch, backed by the same repository

questions.explanation: Worktrees are extra checkouts of one repo: each has its own files and branch, sharing the underlying history. One agent per worktree = filesystem isolation without cloning.

questions.prompt: You're fanning three agents out over a codebase. Which task split is best?

options.text: All three refactor the same core module from different angles
Independent chunks: one takes the API layer, one the UI components, one the test suite — minimal shared files
Each rewrites the whole app; keep the best
One works while two watch for mistakes

questions.explanation: Parallel speedup depends on independence. Overlapping edits (a) reconverge as merge conflicts; triplicating everything (c) triples cost for one output.

questions.prompt: What remains YOUR job when running parallel agents? (select all that apply)

options.text: Designing the split so tasks don't overlap
Resolving conflicts when isolation wasn't perfect
Nothing — parallel agents manage and merge themselves

questions.explanation: Parallelism multiplies output and review load together. Task design, review, and merging are the human bottleneck — and the quality gate.
